📌 Old Token Approvals: The Permission You Forgot You Gave

Main Points
⏺ Many dApps ask you to "approve" a token before you can swap, lend or stake it
⏺ That approval often stays active long after you stop using the app
⏺ This post explains why old approvals are risky and how to clean them up




1️⃣ Core Idea — An approval lets a smart contract move a specific token from your wallet on your behalf. Some apps request an unlimited amount so you don't have to approve again.
2️⃣ Why It Happens — Approvals don't expire by default. If that contract is later hacked, or you signed an approval on a fake site, the attacker can use it to take the tokens without asking you again.
3️⃣ Example — You used a small DEX two years ago and approved unlimited USDC. The DEX is now abandoned. If its contract is exploited, any USDC in that wallet is exposed, even though you never visit the site anymore.
4️⃣ Red Flags — "Unlimited" approvals for a one-time swap, approval requests from sites you reached through DMs or ads, and wallets that have dozens of approvals you don't recognize.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — Approve only the amount you need, review your approvals regularly in a trusted approval checker or your wallet, and revoke the ones you no longer use. Keep long-term savings in a wallet that doesn't connect to dApps.
Final Thoughts

An approval is a key you hand to a contract. Taking back old keys costs a small fee — losing the tokens costs much more.

The EU Rejects the Reason, Not the Rate

The Trump administration proposed a 15% tariff on all EU goods on Nov. 25, after an investigation by the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) concluded that the EU and 13 other economies fuel a global glut of manufactured goods. Brussels rejected the diagnosis. European Commission spokesman Olof Gill said Europe is “among those most exposed to overcapacity,” which he blamed mainly on state-driven production in third countries.

The tariff is a proposal, and Washington has opened it to public comment. Irish minister Helen McEntee said the findings put no new tariffs in place and that the current 10% rate remains for now. Her initial reading is that the figure respects the July 2025 deal between Trump and Ursula von der Leyen, which capped U.S. tariffs on EU goods at 15%.

The Commission is not threatening retaliation. It says it will study the findings and expects the U.S. to honor the 15% ceiling in full, including when new duties are combined with existing ones. Washington says it counts existing duties within that ceiling. The notice also leaves open a rate of up to 20% if USTR judges the consultations with Brussels unsatisfactory.

Bernd Lange, chair of the European Parliament’s trade committee, called the findings “absurd.” He says that after the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s sweeping emergency tariffs, the president is looking for another legal basis to pressure partners for concessions. That is Lange’s reading, but it fits the timeline.

Brussels is contesting the justification but not the number, at least for now.

📣 MEXC shuts down Visa-linked crypto card less than three months after launch 

🌐 Cryptocurrency exchange MEXC has announced that it will discontinue its Global Card payment services on Nov. 18 at 15:30 UTC, less than two weeks after U.S. authorities issued an order restricting its access to the American financial system. The exchange did not identify the issuing partner or specify whether its decision was directly related to the recent enforcement action by the U.S. Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN).

📊 During the maintenance period, customers could transfer their remaining card balances to their exchange accounts, while transactions initiated before the suspension remained subject to normal settlement procedures. MEXC had initially described the interruption as temporary but has now confirmed that the service will not resume as scheduled.

🔗 Cardholders could receive cashback ranging from 4% to 10%, with monthly rewards capped at up to 800 USDT depending on their eligibility. Applications were already unavailable to U.S. residents under the exchange’s regional restrictions. Customers using the card for recurring payments have been advised to cancel their subscriptions or register alternative payment methods to avoid interruptions once the card becomes inactive.

Bybit has declined to release a full postmortem on the $1.4B hack, leaving out detailed data and a complete account of what happened.

That decision has raised concerns, as a postmortem can help users understand the cause of an incident and the steps taken to address it. With no full report available, questions remain about the breach and its aftermath, making it difficult to assess the risks of keeping large sums on the exchange.

🦅 THE 1916 DESIGN STILL SHINING ON AMERICA'S SILVER EAGLE

In 1916, the Mint introduced a new half dollar by sculptor Adolph A. Weinman. Lady Liberty strides toward the dawn of a new day, the Stars and Stripes flying behind her.

The Walking Liberty half dollar was struck in 90% silver from 1916 to 1947.

But Weinman's Liberty came back. On November 24, 1986, the United States Mint released the first American Silver Eagle, the nation's official silver bullion coin, with the Walking Liberty design on its front.

Each Silver Eagle contains one troy ounce of .999 fine silver, and Weinman's Liberty is still struck today, 110 years after she first appeared.
